title: Uber Cuts 10% of Customer Service Jobs as AI Overhaul Reshapes Operations
excerpt: The ride-hailing giant is eliminating roughly one in ten customer service roles, citing its growing 'embrace' of artificial intelligence — the latest in a string of workforce restructuring moves that have accompanied Uber's aggressive AI adoption.
body:
Customer Service Hit by AI Restructuring

Uber Technologies is eliminating roughly 10% of its customer service positions as the company restructures operations around artificial intelligence, Bloomberg reported. The cuts come as Uber's customer service division deploys AI agents to handle an increasing share of rider and driver support queries, replacing human-written policies with automated systems trained on desired outcomes.

https://x.com/rohanpaul_ai/status/2080182745657987401

In an internal communication, the company described parts of the affected organisation as having become "too complex and siloed," according to reports in Moneycontrol and India Today. The restructuring aims to streamline support operations and reduce overlap between human agents and AI-powered systems.

A Pattern of AI-Adjacent Cuts

The customer service reductions follow a broader pattern of workforce restructuring at Uber in 2026. In early June, the company cut 23% of its "People and Places" division — the team responsible for HR, recruiting, and facilities — affecting less than 1% of Uber's approximately 34,000 employees.

Uber President Jill Hazelbaker, who was promoted from chief marketing officer in May, said those cuts were meant to create a "more connected, modern, operationally excellent organisation." CEO Dara Khosrowshahi backed the restructuring, telling company leaders that the changes were "necessary to maximise the effectiveness" of the affected teams, according to Bloomberg.

"The trade-off is going to be headcount. We are budgeting differently. Previously you would have a headcount budget or plan… Now there's an active trade-off going on between the two."

— Dara Khosrowshahi, Uber CEO, on The Verge's Decoder podcast

The AI Budget Blowout

The cuts arrive against the backdrop of Uber's turbulent relationship with AI spending. The company exhausted its entire 2026 AI coding budget by April — just four months into the fiscal year — after encouraging employees to adopt tools like Anthropic's Claude Code and Cursor as aggressively as possible.

Uber responded by capping employee AI spending at $1,500 per month per agentic coding tool, according to TechCrunch. The company has also deployed internal dashboards to track AI usage and created a formal review process for engineers needing to exceed the limits.

About 95% of Uber's engineers now use AI coding tools monthly, and roughly 10% of the company's code is now generated autonomously by AI agents, according to the company's May earnings call. CEO Khosrowshahi has said those productivity gains are allowing Uber to "moderate the overall pace of hiring relative to its plans entering the year."

Questions About AI Returns

Not everyone in Uber's C-suite is convinced the spending is paying off. COO Andrew Macdonald said during a podcast appearance that it is "very hard to draw a line" between AI usage and the delivery of useful features to customers. He described the AI investment as "harder to justify" as the gap between spending and measurable productivity persists.

The tension between aggressive adoption and uncertain returns reflects a broader industry reckoning. Companies from Microsoft to Walmart have imposed similar AI spending controls in recent months, and a Morningstar analysis found that busted AI budgets are, paradoxically, making human workers look cheaper in some cases.

What It Means for Workers in India

Uber's customer service operations span multiple countries, including significant operations in India where the company maintains large support centres. While Uber has not disclosed a geographic breakdown of the affected roles, the restructuring raises questions about the future of customer service outsourcing — a sector that employs hundreds of thousands of workers across Indian cities.

With Uber's stock down roughly 14% year to date and AI's return on investment increasingly under scrutiny, the company's next moves will be closely watched by both investors and the workforce that powers its global operations.
